blocks.title: Luminosity
blocks.text: Luminosity, L, is the total amount of energy emitted by a star per unit time as electromagnetic radiation: the total power of radiation emitted by the star, measured in watts. It defines the intrinsic brightness of a star.

A star's luminosity depends mainly on its radius and its surface temperature. Larger stars have more surface area to emit radiation and so tend to be more luminous; of two stars of equal size, the one with the higher surface temperature radiates more energy. The luminosity is the product of the surface area, A = 4 pi r^2, and the power radiated per unit area, sigma T^4: L = 4 pi r^2 sigma T^4 (21.1). This is the Stefan-Boltzmann law: the total output power of a star is proportional to the product of its surface area and the fourth power of its temperature. Here sigma is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, 5.67 x 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4, T the surface temperature and r the radius of the star.

blocks.title: Tidbit and do you know?
blocks.text: The Sun shines with an immense luminosity of about 4 x 10^26 watts, equivalent to billions of nuclear explosions every second. The Stefan-Boltzmann law helps astronomers estimate the size and brightness of stars just by knowing their temperature.

The luminosity of a star is 2.5 x 10^26 W and its surface temperature is 6000 K. Estimate the radius of the star. Solution: from L = 4 pi r^2 sigma T^4, r = square root of [L / (4 pi sigma T^4)] = square root of [2.5 x 10^26 W / (4 x 3.14 x 5.67 x 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4 x (6000 K)^4)] = 5.2 x 10^8 m.
If a star becomes twice as hot (its size unchanged), how many times more energy will it radiate?
